lead: String instructions process a block byte by byte using SI, DI and CX. Control transfer instructions change IP, or CS and IP. A hand-written copy loop is long and slow, so REP with the direction flag lets one instruction copy, compare, scan, load or store a block. Jumps, calls, returns, loops and interrupts steer the program; CALL and RET use the stack to save return addresses. These instructions appear in memory copy, display buffers, serial buffers and delay loops. Only a few universities teach string instructions separately; some syllabi group these under advanced instructions.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.3 for 8086 registers and flags, and Unit 3 for addressing modes and the stack.

sections.h3: String instructions and the direction flag

blocks.text: String instructions treat memory as a block. The source address is DS:SI: DS is the data segment base and SI is the source index. The destination address is ES:DI: ES is the extra segment base and DI is the destination index. CX holds the count. DF, the direction flag, picks the step: DF = 0 means SI and DI increase after each byte or word; DF = 1 means they decrease. MOVS copies: MOVSB moves one byte from [SI] to [DI], MOVSW moves one word. CMPS compares the byte or word at [DS:SI] with the one at [ES:DI] and sets the flags as if the source were subtracted from the destination; SCAS compares AL or AX with [ES:DI] and sets the flags the same way. LODS loads AL or AX from [SI]. STOS stores AL or AX to [DI]. REP repeats while CX ≠ 0 and decrements CX after each move. REPE and REPNE repeat CMPS or SCAS while ZF is 1 or 0, and stop early when the condition fails or CX reaches zero. They are used for block copy, screen buffers and serial receive buffers.

sections.h3: Control transfer: jumps, calls and returns

blocks.text: Control transfer instructions change the instruction pointer. A near JMP loads IP only; a far JMP loads CS and IP. Conditional jumps read flags: JZ tests ZF = 1, JNZ ZF = 0, JC CF = 1, JNC CF = 0, JS and JNS test SF, JO and JNO test OF. Unsigned comparisons use JA and JB; signed comparisons use JG and JL. LOOP decrements CX and jumps if CX ≠ 0; LOOPE and LOOPNE also test ZF. CALL saves a return address on the stack. A near CALL pushes IP, so SP = SP − 2. A far CALL pushes CS, then IP, so SP = SP − 4. RET pops IP for a near return; RETF pops IP and CS. The stack grows down, so every push lowers SP. INT n pushes FLAGS, clears IF and TF, pushes CS, pushes IP, then loads CS:IP from the interrupt vector table at address n × 4. IRET reverses this and restores flags. A delay loop uses a count register with LOOP or DEC/JNZ.

figure.caption: REP MOVSB repeats the byte move until CX reaches zero; DF decides whether SI and DI step up or down.

spec.title: REP MOVSB loop
spec.aria: A REP MOVSB loop: copy one byte from [DS:SI] to [ES:DI], step SI and DI up if DF = 0 or down if DF = 1, decrement CX, and repeat until CX is 0.

examples.question: A string of 5 bytes starts at DS:SI = 2000H:0100H. Assume ES = 2000H, DI = 3000H, CX = 0005H and DF = 0. Give the physical addresses of the source and destination, and the values of SI, DI and CX after one MOVSB.
steps: MOVSB copies one byte from [DS:SI] to [ES:DI], then updates the pointers according to DF.
DF = 0, so SI and DI increase: SI = 0100H + 1 = 0101H = 257; DI = 3000H + 1 = 3001H = 12289.
CX counts down after the move: CX = 0005H − 1 = 0004H = 4.
examples.check:
ds=0x2000
si=0x0100
es=0x2000
di=0x3000
cx=0x0005
src=ds*16+si
dst=es*16+di
si2=si+1
di2=di+1
cx2=cx-1
print(src)
print(dst)
print(si2)
print(di2)
print(cx2)

traps: MOVS destination is always ES:DI, not DS:DI. If ES is not given, the destination physical address cannot be found; many questions set ES = DS.
DF = 0 increments SI and DI; DF = 1 decrements them. Reversing this changes every address after the first byte.
CX decrements after the move, so after one byte it is count − 1, not count. REP tests CX at the start of each repeat.
A near CALL pushes only IP (2 bytes); a far CALL pushes CS and IP (4 bytes). A matching RET or RETF must be used.

quiz.q: Which registers hold the source and destination addresses in MOVSB?
quiz.a: Source is DS:SI; destination is ES:DI.

quiz.q: Why does REP MOVSB need fewer instruction fetches than a hand-written copy loop?
quiz.a: The repeat is handled by the processor, so one instruction replaces the move, pointer update, compare and jump sequence.

quiz.q: CX = 0003H, DF = 1, SI = 0200H, DI = 0400H. Give SI, DI and CX after one MOVSB.
A near CALL executes at CS:IP = 1000H:0200H and pushes a return address. What is on the stack and how does SP change?
quiz.a: SP = SP − 2, and the word at the new [SP] holds the return offset 0203H (the near CALL at 0200H is 3 bytes long); CS is not pushed, so execution returns to 1000H:0203H.

quiz.q: A loop body is between label L and LOOP L. CX = 0002H at entry. How many times does the body run?
quiz.a: Two times. The first LOOP makes CX = 1 and jumps; the second makes CX = 0 and falls through.

quiz.q: When does REPE CMPS stop before CX reaches zero?
quiz.a: It stops when ZF = 0, because REPE continues while equal (ZF = 1).

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern x86 processors still keep string instructions, but fast block moves often use wider loads, DMA or library routines. Operating systems use REP MOVSB for small copies and switch to other methods for large ones. The 8086 segment pair DS:SI and ES:DI still appears in x86 memory models and emulators. Search for ERMSB, REP MOVSB performance, and x86 interrupt vector table.
